meta.title: The machines are fine. I'm worried about us
meta.author: edsu

comments.author: lonjil
comments.text:
I think this essay was written by AI. There's a Dune quote:


Frank Herbert (yeah, I know I'm a nerd), in God Emperor of Dune, has a character observe: "What do such machines really do? They increase the number of things we can do without thinking. Things we do without thinking; there's the real danger." Herbert was writing science fiction. I'm writing about my office. The distance between those two things has gotten uncomfortably small.


The original text in the book uses an em-dash, but this quote uses a semicolon instead. A plausible explanation is that at least some of the text in this article was generated by an LLM, which being trained on quality writing, used a few em-dashes, that were then replaced by semicolons to make the text seem "less AI".

comments.author: gf0
comments.text:
Come on, these "takes" are getting spam level useless.. "written by AI" mean something entirely different than "have probably used AI in small parts" to e.g. check for typos, improve grammar and readability (you may want to look at the part where the author talks about how not being a native English speaker puts someone at a disadvantage in academia - and this being democratized by LLMs).

Also, selecting from a PDF reader may do OCR which could explain the dash replace, or they may have manually copied a quote (I have done that with short quotes when the source was some scanned book where naive OCR produced garbage). Does it make the article less worthy?

Also, from the article:


I should be honest about the context I'm writing from, because this essay would be obnoxious coming from someone who's never touched an LLM. I use AI agents regularly


It's a very well written and informative article well worth a read. You are free to ignore it, but then don't spam the comment section with baseless claims, discouraging others from reading it. If it were AI slop, then it should be flagged and removed.

comments.author: muvlon
comments.text: It is deeply ironic and disturbing for an AI to be writing "the machines are fine, I'm worried about us [humans]" type blog posts. Like fuck you skinwalker, you are not one of us.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
That's another problem with AIs. Now we are going to be double checking and doubting everything because it could have maybe was written by AI.

My only problem with this article is that it should have been two paragraphs tops. Was AI used in creating this waste of time, doesn't bother me.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
I will just note that in my judgment, this is almost certainly LLM-written. This is based both on a subjective reading and on a check with Pangram (which is a remarkably good, conservative LLM text detector). I'm not saying you need to hate it, but maybe calibrate the effort you're spending on reading and arguing with the article with the effort the author probably did not put into writing it.

More generally, I'm finding that 50%+ of pro- and anti-AI think pieces in my feed appear to be LLM-written. People obviously have strong opinions about the topic, and it's easy to get them to upvote low-effort articles that say the things they want to hear.

comments.author: addison
comments.text:
I hate that I (1) need such a radar, and (2) do not. This makes me not want to engage with untrusted content at all, because every time I have the rug pulled out from under me like this, it feels like personal disrespect to my time and effort reading.

I cannot express just how much I wish for this bubble to burst (both economically and socially). I would say that I can't wait for people to go back to writing things for people rather than generating content for views, but that'd be a severe case of rose-tinted glasses. I do miss it at least being a bit more distinguishable.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Yeah, apologies for sharing this here. It wasn't meant to be a rugpull -- I loathe them too.

I generally agreed with the author's argument that unless you are trained in the scientific process  you will not be able to evaluate machines that are simulating engagement in the scientific process--and that the need for that isn't going to go away. If the author was an LLM, or a person augmented with an LLM I think the argument still stands.

comments.author: addison
comments.text: Whether it is a valid argument or not, it is completely undermined by the author's choice to doctor his own engagement with the topic with an LLM. Using one to "clean up" one's words (or, worse, generate them), is seemingly completely antithetical to the claim. The utter disingenuousness of it has earned an entry in my uBlock.

comments.author: gf0
comments.text: Why? How do you know they are not non-English speakers using LLMs to "even the field" of writing blog posts? Is that "antithetical"? Is my phone auto-correct also problematic in your view?

comments.author: addison
comments.text: This is irrelevant, and a strawman IMO. LLMs are a comprehensively different technology with enormous ethical and labour connotations. It is the means of pedagogical corruption. I would prefer imperfect writing to anything "corrected" by this; indeed, in my workplace, I am the only native English speaker -- and our job is producing technical writing in English. The human who has the opinion matters, not the correctness of the writing.

comments.author: dsr
comments.text: I am in agreement with the essence of the argument: productive work requires that some person understand the system; using LLMs to replace understanding the system defeats the ability to supervise them.

comments.author: quad
comments.text:
The trajectory, from the outside, was identical.


Ahh, the 'ol Chinese cubicle thought experiment.

comments.author: sloane
comments.text:
re: substance, i think i agree broadly with the thrust.

re: the provenance of this article, i must admit that i didn’t detect any LLM tells on my first, not so close reading of it. but then, i haven’t really focused on my distinguishing/discriminating abilities all that much. the commentary on bluesky is largely positive, although i see one commenter say it read like Claude’s writing.

re: the overlap of substance and provenance, is it possible this author wrote some parts of the text themselves and delegated others? i’m curious if their (potential) usage of LLMs in writing this article is something they see as separate from their usage of LLMs in doing physics work, likely reducing their qualms about relying very heavily on Claude, or connected to they way they use it in their physics work—is it possible this article was heavily edited with Claude, rather than generated out of whole cloth? i am tempted to reach out to the author and ask about their writing process and thoughts.

comments.author: sjamaan
comments.text:
my first, not so close reading of it


That's the thing, right? LLMs produce so much verbiage that it turns a blog-length article into a book-length one. So you sort of have to skim. The sheer length of the text combined with the fluffy writing style obscures the point.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
I don't mind when people use LLMs as editors. But when I encounter a suspiciously-looking article, I ask myself what's the minimum amount of text you'd need to enter to have an an LLM produce a functionally identical post.

A lot of LLM-generated blog posts can be boiled down to really short prompts ("generate an article about the importance of Immanuel Kant in the age of AI", etc). It's not a proof of AI slop, but if I see a combination of LLM output + shallow thesis + no prior human-like content from the author... you know, life's too short to engage?

And remember that the article talks about the subtle, negative consequences of relying on LLMs to do the grunt work, so even if it's just heavily AI-edited, what's that supposed to mean?

comments.author: sloane
comments.text: that’s very fair, and the author’s lack of existing online “casual” (non-academic) writing could be taken as evidence that they wouldn’t be doing writing like this if not for LLM assistance. not that that means it’s all generated, heavily edited, or anything necessarily, but it certainly makes arriving at a different conclusion more difficult.
